newsitem.title: USA: Army secretary launches probe of sex scandal.
newsitem.headline: Army secretary launches probe of sex scandal.

text.p: The U.S. Army on Friday launched a high-level investigation of the sex scandal shaking its ranks, including whether any top officers should be held responsible for the rape and harassment of female recruits.

"We will go wherever the evidence takes us," Army Secretary Togo West told reporters when asked if senior officers might be sacked if they condoned an atmosphere where females could be sexually abused by male drill instructors.
"We will not be hesitant to take the steps that information we develop dictates," he said, while stressing he did not think "heads should roll" just to drive home a point.

Since the scandal broke two weeks ago, at least 10 drill instructors and other trainers have been charged with violations ranging from rape to "fraternizing" with female recruits at the Army's Aberdeen Proving Ground in Maryland and and at Fort Leonard Wood in Missouri.

The scandal hit hard in the Pentagon, which has pressed to improve treatment of women in uniform since the Navy's 1991 "Tailhook" scandal in which male Navy and Marine pilots abused females at a Las Vegas hotel.

West named a high-level advisory panel of officers and civilians to look into the handling of sexual abuse and ordered a separate probe by Army Inspector General Jared Bates, a lieutenant general and the Army's top legal officer.
Bates will "assess the responsibility and accountability of the chain of command" in addition to focusing on confidence of soldiers' in the Army's "no tolerance" policy on abuse.
The advisory panel will be led by Retired Maj. Gen. Richard Siegfried, who will be called back to active duty, and will provide a preliminary report to West within 120 days.
It will determine how the Army can better fight its war against sexual harassment, including perhaps early and clear advice to young female recruits of their rights as soldiers.
West noted that the Army had already received 5,000 calls on newly established sexual abuse "hotline" and that 600 had been turned over to its Criminal Investigation Division.
"At bottom, the violations we are looking at are violations of clear rules of law on the one hand and the way leaders conduct themselves on the other," said West, a lawyer.

Since the scandal broke at Aberdeen, the Army has begun investigating possible harassment of young recruits at all of its training bases, and Defence Secretary William Perry has ordered each service to re-examine its policies on harassment.
Meanwhile, House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich has ordered a congressional review to learn if Navy, Air Force or Marine instructors have sexually abused female recruits.

The 1991 convention of the "Tailhook Association" of Navy and Marine fliers in Las Vegas resulted in the dismissal of a number of senior Navy and Marine officers, including admirals, and the resignation of then-Navy Secretary Lawrence Garrett.
The Navy's top officer, Adm. Frank Kelso, also took early retirement less than three years later, saying he had become a "lightning rod" in the long investigation of Tailhook.
